title: Numerically exact simulation of open quantum networks with strong system-bath couplings using tensor network path integrals
abstract: Non-Markovian open quantum networks are among the most challenging problems in quantum theory, as they suffer from both, the exponentially scaling many-body state space as well as long memory times when the sites are strongly coupled to structured environments. Recent efforts to address them by combining tensor networks with real-time path integrals, such as TEMPO and process tensors, were however limited to systems with rather weak system-environment couplings because strong couplings lead to large bond dimensions. Here, we devise a tensor network scheme (CTEMPO) resulting in particularly small bond dimensions for single-site problems. We then extend this to a practical scheme to simulate non-Markovian quantum networks by time-evolving a corresponding comb tensor network. Benchmarking the single-site algorithm on the spin-boson model we find orders-of-magnitude improvement over established methods. The multi-site algorithm is shown to solve the notoriously difficult problem of the 7-site Fenna-Matthews-Olson photosynthetic complex, whose spectral density contains 62 peaks. We then apply our approach to explore the scaling behavior of the superradiance of up to $N=20$ quantum dots individually coupled to super-Ohmic phonon baths. Our approach provides a turnkey solution to non-Markovian quantum networks and is compatible with more general tensor network topologies.
summary: This paper introduces CTEMPO, a novel tensor network path integral method designed for numerically exact simulation of open quantum systems with strong coupling. It overcomes the limitations of previous techniques by maintaining small bond dimensions, enabling the study of complex models like photosynthetic complexes and large quantum dot arrays. This provides a turnkey solution for non-Markovian quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of numerically simulating non-Markovian open quantum networks, especially those involving strong system-bath couplings, which typically lead to exponentially scaling state spaces.
main_result: The proposed CTEMPO scheme provides a significant computational speed-up (orders of magnitude) over established methods like TEMPO and PT-MPO, allowing for the simulation of complex systems like the 7-site FMO complex and large QD arrays.
method: The core method is CTEMPO, a novel tensor network path integral scheme that combines insights from TEMPO and causal contraction order to maintain small bond dimensions when simulating the time evolution of the system density matrix.
model_or_system: The work applies to general open quantum networks, including the spin-boson model, the 7-site Fenna-Matthews-Olson (FMO) photosynthetic complex, and arrays of quantum dots (QDs) coupled to structured phonon baths.
key_observables: Time evolution of expectation values (e.g., $\langle \sigma_z angle$), superradiant emission intensity, and computational metrics like bond dimensions ($\chi$) and run time.
important_parameters: Strong coupling regimes ($\alpha=1$), spectral density structure (super-Ohmic), and system size ($N$ up to 20 QDs).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the environment coupling can be effectively mapped onto a tensor network structure, and the simulation is limited by available computer memory for very large systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the tensor network structure comparison (CTEMPO vs. others), the time evolution of $\langle \sigma_z angle$ showing performance gains, and the superradiant emission intensity decay curves.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the CTEMPO algorithm and its multi-site extension (comb tensor network), validates it by benchmarking against existing methods on the spin-boson model, and then applies it to complex physical systems like FMO and QDs.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it provides a powerful, scalable numerical tool to simulate open quantum dynamics in complex, strongly coupled environments where standard methods fail due to memory or computational cost.
